doc.title: Duffy Jackson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 17, 1995

title: The Life magazine jazz photograph earlier that day
summary: Monk Rowe opens the filming; Duffy describes taking part that day in a Life magazine photo of jazz greats taken by Gordon Parks, linked to his father's Great Day in Harlem connection.

story.theme_name: Opening the interview: Monk Rowe's welcome and archive boilerplate
story.community_name: Opening the Hamilton College interview: introductions and boilerplate

blocks.x: We are filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive and we’re very happy to have with us Duffy Jackson — drummer, singer, bass player — I know it’s on your resume.
I’m a jack of all trades, master of some, I don’t know.
And it’s a great pleasure to have you here.
Would you like to tell us about what you were doing today?

This is the most incredible day of my life it seems, and I’ve had a few very interesting occasions in the history of music, being the son of a bass player. You know my dad, Chubby Jackson, has permitted me to exist in some very unique musical environments and situations, but today I was very, very honored to be part of a photograph for Life magazine of the greatest musicians of all time in the history of jazz. There were hundreds of them actually. I mean they were only supposed to have around maybe eighty musicians originally scheduled, but then all of a sudden the word got out and everyone wanted to be part of it. It was an opportunity to meet and greet and hug and kiss a whole bunch of the great masters of our American music. And I’ve been big fans of every one of them and there are a bunch of the younger contingent out there too, and just to meet them in a casual way and to exchange phone numbers and hugs and stuff like that, it was a very meaningful experience. I was permitted, through my dad’s association with A Great Day In Harlem movie, where yesterday they went back to that same spot up there, uptown, and took a picture with the remaining survivors.
